title: Marketing and Social Media
promise: Turn social posting into a chain: calendar, AI-generated pieces, brand review, and approval before anything goes out.
audience: local businesses, personal brands, small agencies, and communications leads at an organization
plain: This is a miniature newsroom for your social media. Instead of sitting down every morning wondering "what do I post today?", the system works backward: first you decide a monthly calendar with the topics and formats, and from there AI drafts the texts, proposes the image, and puts everything in a review queue. A person looks at each piece, checks it sounds like your brand and not a template, corrects it if needed, and approves it. Only then does it get scheduled. Nothing goes out published without someone having read it, because a bad tweet can be deleted but a screenshot can't. The point isn't publishing more: it's publishing consistently without it eating two hours of your day, and measuring at month's end what really worked so you do more of that and less of everything else. The same circuit works for a restaurant, a shop, a firm, or your personal brand: the tone and topics change, the mechanics don't.
fits: Businesses that post "whenever they remember" and haven't posted anything in three weeks
A solo communications lead running four networks and falling behind
Local brands that want a steady presence on Instagram and Facebook without hiring an agency
Small agencies managing several client accounts and repeating the same work every month
Teams that already have a blog or newsletter and want to break it into pieces for social
Shops that need pieces for seasonal campaigns: sales, Christmas, back-to-school
Professionals' personal brands (lawyers, nutritionists, trainers) who want to post two or three times a week
Organizations with several people weighing in on every post and no approval process
Anyone who wants to know which posts work and today never looks at a metric
Teams that reply to comments and messages late because nobody's been assigned them
notFor: Reputation crisis management. If you have a fire on social media, that's handled by an experienced person in real time, not a workflow
Publishing automatically with no human review. This kit doesn't do that and you shouldn't build it: a piece with a made-up fact published overnight is very expensive
Buying followers, automating likes, or sending unsolicited mass messages. Besides being useless, it can cost you the account
Paid advertising (Meta Ads, Google Ads). That's a different trade with a different budget; this kit covers organic content
Brands with nothing to say. If there's no business, story, or point of view behind it, AI just generates filler faster

scopes.label: Minimum
scopes.what: A monthly calendar in a spreadsheet, text generation with AI from a prompt carrying your tone, and manual review: you copy, adjust, and publish by hand. No workflow yet.
scopes.cost: €0/month with free plans, plus cents of API cost
scopes.skip: Skip automatic scheduling and metrics. With the calendar and drafts you already cut 70% of the time each post takes.

scopes.label: Standard
scopes.what: Everything in Minimum plus the n8n workflow: every morning it reads the calendar, generates the piece, runs it through an automatic brand filter, and sends it for approval. What's approved gets marked ready to schedule.
scopes.time: Two weeks in spare moments, about 15 hours
scopes.skip: Skip automatic image generation and the monthly report. Start with text and a fixed Canva template.

scopes.label: Advanced
scopes.what: Everything above plus image generation with brand review, scheduling via your scheduling tool's API, weekly metrics collection into the sheet, and a monthly report saying what to repeat and what to stop.
scopes.time: A month and a half part-time
scopes.cost: €60-150/month depending on scheduling tools and volume
scopes.skip: Don't start here. API scheduling and metrics only make sense once you've spent a month approving pieces and know your correction rate.

brief.name: Define your strategy before generating anything
brief.when: First thing. Before asking AI for a single post, before opening n8n.
brief.prompt:
Act as a down-to-earth content strategist. We're going to build a social posting system with AI and human approval, and I want you to first force me to define the strategy, not the tools.

My context:
- Business or brand: [BUSINESS]
- Who I want to reach and what I want that person to do: [AUDIENCE AND GOAL]
- Networks I'm on or want to be on: [NETWORKS]
- What I've posted the last two months and how it went: [HISTORY]
- Brand tone, with real examples of my own phrases: [TONE]
- Who reviews and approves each piece: [APPROVER]
- Hours per week and budget per month: [LIMITS]
- Topics I NEVER want to talk about: [BANNED]

Do this, in this order:

1. Give me my situation back summarized in five lines and flag every assumption you're making with WARNING.
2. Ask me only the three questions that would most change the strategy. Stop and wait for my answer.
3. Once I answer, tell me which networks are NOT worth being on with my resources and why. Be restrictive: two networks done well beats five done halfway.
4. Propose three content pillars (the topics that repeat every week) with the proportion between them, and a specific format per pillar.
5. Tell me the realistic frequency for my hours: how many pieces a week I can sustain for six months without burning out.
6. Write the 90-day success criteria with a number that isn't followers: messages received, clicks to the website, bookings, attributed sales.

Don't give me a calendar yet. Don't write me any post yet. If you think this isn't sustainable with my resources, tell me and say what you'd cut.

fill.what: What you sell and to whom, in two lines
fill.example: Physiotherapy clinic in Zaragoza, three physios, patients aged 30-60

fill.what: The specific person and the action you want to prompt
fill.example: People with back pain from office work; want them to book via WhatsApp

fill.what: Where you are today and with what numbers
fill.example: Instagram with 800 followers, Facebook abandoned, nothing else

fill.what: What you posted and what worked, even from memory
fill.example: Tip carousels, an exercise video that got 4,000 views, shop photos nobody saw

fill.what: How you talk. Paste three of your real sentences, not adjectives
fill.example: "Back pain isn't cured with a brace, it's cured by moving." Friendly, direct, no jargon, informal

fill.what: Who gives final approval to each piece
fill.example: Myself; if it's about health, my partner also reviews it

fill.what: Real weekly hours and euros per month
fill.example: Three hours a week and under €40/month

fill.what: Forbidden topics: legal, sensitive, or just not you
fill.example: Politics, cure promises, comparisons with other clinics

brief.expect: Your situation summarized with warnings, three questions, and then: ruled-out networks, three pillars with proportions, sustainable frequency, and a success criterion that isn't followers.
brief.stuck: If it hands you a 30-day calendar right away, it didn't listen: reply "I didn't ask for a calendar, ask me the three questions from point 2 and wait." A strategy with no answers from you is a template.

architecture.what: The sheet where the plan lives: what's posted, on what day, on which network, under which pillar, and what state each piece is in.
architecture.nocode: Google Sheets with one row per piece and a status column.
architecture.code: A table in Postgres or Airtable with views by status.
architecture.why: The calendar rules. Without it, AI generates loose pieces with no direction and you're back to "what do I post today?" that you came here to kill.

architecture.what: The model writes the piece from the calendar's row: topic, pillar, network, and your tone guide.
architecture.nocode: An HTTP Request node against the model's API with the kit's drafting prompt.
architecture.code: The official SDK with the tone guide as a versioned system prompt in the repository.
architecture.why: The tone guide lives in the prompt, not in anyone's head. It's what makes Monday's draft and Thursday's sound like the same brand.

architecture.what: The visual proposal: a generated image or a brand template filled with the piece's text.
architecture.nocode: Canva templates filled by hand, or generation with an image tool from a brief the model writes.
architecture.code: A call to the image API with the generated brief, saving the result to a per-month folder.
architecture.why: The image is where a lack of brand shows the most. A well-made fixed template beats a differently generated image every day.

architecture.what: A second AI pass that checks the piece against your rule list: tone, banned topics, unsourced claims, too many emoji.
architecture.nocode: A second HTTP Request node with the brand-review prompt. If it fails, the piece goes back to the queue with the reason.
architecture.code: A validation function that returns pass or fail with reasons, before the human queue.
architecture.why: This filter doesn't replace the person: it saves them from reviewing the obviously bad. The person reviews what already passed the filter.

architecture.what: The point where a person reads the whole piece, corrects it, or approves it. Nothing gets scheduled without passing through here.
architecture.nocode: A Slack message with the whole piece and two buttons, or a status column in the sheet someone changes by hand.
architecture.code: A pending queue with a screen showing text and image together.
architecture.why: This is the kit's red line. A bad piece in a drawer costs nothing; published, it costs reputation. Approval is cheap by comparison.

architecture.what: Passing the approved piece to the tool that will publish it at its time: Metricool, Buffer, Meta's native scheduler.
architecture.nocode: At first, by hand: you copy the approved piece to your scheduler once a week, in a short session.
architecture.code: A call to the scheduler's API from the workflow, only with pieces in approved status.
architecture.why: Separating approving from scheduling lets you batch: you approve pieces during the week and schedule all of them on Friday in twenty minutes.

architecture.what: Collecting each week the reach, engagement, and clicks from what's published, and logging them next to each calendar piece.
architecture.nocode: Exporting the platform's or scheduler's stats to the sheet, one column per metric.
architecture.code: Scheduled calls to the stats API, writing into the same calendar table.
architecture.why: The metric attached to the piece is what turns this into a system that learns: you see which pillar works and adjust next month's calendar with data.

stack.nocode: n8n, self-hosted or cloud. Reads the calendar, calls the model, and requests approval.
stack.code: A cron-triggered Python script that does the same.
stack.pick: n8n. Seeing each run with the generated piece inside is worth gold when one goes wrong and you have to explain why.

stack.need: The model that drafts and reviews
stack.nocode: HTTP call to the Anthropic or OpenAI API with the key in n8n credentials.
stack.code: The official SDK, with the tone guide as a system prompt.
stack.pick: A mid-size model for drafting and a small one for the brand filter. Writing well needs nuance; checking rules is cheap.

stack.nocode: Google Sheets: calendario, metricas and guia_marca tabs.
stack.code: Airtable if you want kanban views by status; Postgres if you already have a database.
stack.pick: Sheets. The calendar has to be editable by someone who doesn't know tools, and anyone can edit a sheet.

stack.nocode: Canva with two or three fixed brand templates. For generated images, an image tool with the brief the model writes.
stack.code: Image generation API, with images saved in Drive by month.
stack.pick: Start with Canva templates. A template's visual consistency almost always beats the surprise of a generated image, and doesn't need as fine a brand review.

stack.nocode: Metricool or Buffer on the free plan, or Meta Business Suite's native scheduling (free for Instagram and Facebook).
stack.code: The API of whichever scheduler you pick; each network's direct APIs are a maintenance headache.
stack.pick: Meta Business Suite if you're only on Instagram and Facebook: free and no middleman. A paid scheduler once you have more networks.

stack.nocode: Slack with buttons if the team lives there; if not, the sheet's status column and a daily email reminder.
stack.code: A pending view filtered by status.
stack.pick: Wherever the approver checks every day without you having to remind them. An approval that has to be chased ends up in expired pieces.

fields: The piece's unique identifier, generated when the row is created
The planned publish day, in ISO format
The content pillar it belongs to, from your closed list
The piece's specific topic, in one sentence
The generated text, as it came out or as it ended up after correction
Link to the image or name of the template used
planned, generated, brand_review, pending_approval, approved, scheduled, published, discarded
If the brand filter or the person rejected it, why, in one line
data.note: Status is the column that drives the whole circuit. The workflow only picks up pieces in planned status, and only a person can set approved. If someone writes made-up statuses by hand, the workflow skips them and it looks like it "doesn't work."

fields: Clicks to the link or profile, if the network provides it
Messages, bookings, or sales manually attributed to that piece
data.note: Collect the metric 7 days after publishing, always on the same day count, or you won't be able to compare pieces. The conversions column is filled by hand and it's the only one that pays the bills.

fields: A specific brand rule, in one checkable sentence
A sentence that breaks the rule, to give the filter contrast
data.note: This tab is the contract between you and the AI. The brand filter's prompt is built by reading these rules. When a bad piece slips through, the question is always the same: which rule was missing here? Add it and it's filtered forever.

phases.title: Strategy and brand guide
phases.goal: Know what gets posted, for whom, in what tone, and what's forbidden, all in writing.
phases.deliverable: Operational brand guide: pillars, tone with examples, checkable rules, and a 90-day success criterion.
done: You have three content pillars with their weekly proportion
The tone guide has real example sentences of yours, not adjectives
There's a list of rules and banned topics that fits on one screen
The 90-day success criterion is a number and it isn't followers

steps.title: Review what you've already posted
steps.action: Take your last 20 posts and note in a sheet: topic, format, reach, and engagement. Sort by engagement and look at the top five and bottom five. That's your first real data point.
steps.expect: A pattern, even a rough one: "practical tips work, team photos don't." If there's no pattern, your history is too scattered and the brief will help twice as much.
steps.stuck: If you don't have 20 posts, skip this step guilt-free and lean more on the brief's questions. Don't invent data you don't have.

steps.title: Run the brief and sit through the questions
steps.action: Fill in the kickoff prompt's blanks and paste it. Answer the three questions with real data. Don't let it skip the order.
steps.expect: Ruled-out networks, three pillars with proportions, sustainable frequency, and a numeric success criterion.
steps.stuck: If it proposes five networks and fifteen pieces a week, remind it of your hours: "I have three hours a week, adjust to that." Unsustainable frequency is death sentence number one for these projects.

steps.title: Write the checkable brand guide
steps.action: Turn your tone and bans into one-sentence rules a machine can check: "we never promise health results," "max two emoji per piece," "always informal," "never mention competitors." Add a rule-breaking example to each.
steps.expect: Between 8 and 15 rules. If you have 40, you've written a style manual, not a filter: trim to what actually kills a piece.
steps.stuck: Fire test: give a rule to someone else along with a random piece and ask if it meets it. If they hesitate, the rule isn't checkable. Rewrite it with a clear yes or no.

steps.title: Decide the scope and tell the approver
steps.action: Choose minimum, standard, or advanced. Write which networks, how many pieces per week, and who approves. Show it to the approver and get their explicit yes: they're going to get pieces to review every week.
steps.expect: An agreed paragraph. The approver knows how many pieces will arrive and how long each review takes (2-3 minutes per piece).
steps.stuck: If the approver is a busy boss, agree on a deadline: pieces unreviewed within 48 hours fall off the calendar, they don't publish themselves. Never turn silence into approval.

phases.title: Calendar and first pieces
phases.goal: A month's calendar filled and the first ten pieces generated and hand-corrected, no workflow yet.
phases.deliverable: Monthly calendar with statuses and ten approved pieces that sound like your brand.
done: The calendar has a month of rows with date, network, pillar, and topic
You've generated ten pieces with the drafting prompt and corrected them
The corrections are noted down: you know what the prompt gets wrong
The second batch of pieces needs fewer corrections than the first

steps.title: Build the sheet with its three tabs
steps.action: Create the calendario, metricas, and guia_marca tabs with the exact columns from this kit's data model, lowercase and no accents. Freeze the header row.
steps.nocode: In the status column, add data validation with the closed list of values: Data > Data validation > list of items. This way nobody invents statuses.
steps.expect: Three tabs with headers and the status column with a dropdown.
steps.stuck: If unsure which columns to add, copy the data model's as-is. Adding columns later is easy; renaming them once the workflow already uses them isn't.

steps.title: Fill in the month's calendar
steps.where: Claude or ChatGPT, and your sheet
steps.action: Use the calendar prompt with your pillars and frequency. Review what it returns: remove topics that don't fit you, adjust dates to your real campaigns (sales, events, season), and paste the rows into the sheet with planned status.
steps.expect: A month of specific rows. Every topic is a specific sentence ("3 stretches for after 8 hours sitting"), not a category ("tips").
steps.stuck: If the topics come out generic, give it ammunition: paste the 10 questions your customers ask you most. That's where months of calendar come from.

steps.title: Generate the first ten pieces by hand
steps.action: Take the first ten rows and generate each piece with the drafting prompt. Correct them like you'd correct a talented intern: cross out, rewrite, and note down what type of error repeats.
steps.expect: Ten pieces ready and a list of repeated errors: "too enthusiastic," "always closes with the same phrase," "uses words I don't say."
steps.stuck: If every piece needs a full rewrite, the problem is the prompt's tone guide: feed it three of your old pieces in full as an example. The model imitates examples far better than adjectives.

steps.title: Tune the prompt with what you learned and repeat
steps.action: Turn your error list into prompt rules ("forbidden to close with a rhetorical question," "max one emoji"). Generate five more pieces and compare how much you correct now.
steps.expect: The correction rate visibly drops. If you used to rewrite half, now you're tweaking loose sentences.
steps.stuck: Change a few rules at a time and retest. If you add ten rules at once and it improves, you won't know which ones mattered, and long prompts full of dead rules end up ignored.

steps.title: Solve the image with templates
steps.action: Create two or three brand templates: one for tips, one for quotes or phrases, one for announcements. With your colors, your typeface, and a slot for the headline. For now, each piece's image is a filled-in template.
steps.expect: Three templates anyone can fill in two minutes that read as yours in the feed.
steps.stuck: If you don't have defined colors or a logo, don't try to solve that with AI today: pick two colors and a Canva typeface and be consistent. Consistency beats beauty in a feed.

phases.title: The workflow with brand filter and approval
phases.goal: Have the workflow generate the day's pieces every morning, run them through the brand filter, and send them for approval. Nothing publishes itself.
phases.deliverable: Active n8n workflow: calendar → generated piece → brand filter → human approval → approved status.
done: The workflow triggers itself every morning and picks up the day's planned pieces
The brand filter rejects pieces breaking your rules and notes the reason
The approver receives the full piece and can approve or reject with a button
No piece moves to approved without a human click, and you've checked it on purpose

steps.title: Import the kit's workflow and connect credentials
steps.action: Copy this kit's workflow and use Workflows > Import from clipboard. Connect Google Sheets with your account, create the Header Auth credential for the model (name x-api-key, value your key), and connect Slack.
steps.nocode: In every Sheets node, replace ID_DE_TU_HOJA with your sheet's real identifier: it's in the URL between /d/ and /edit.
steps.expect: The canvas with the twelve nodes connected and no red credential warnings.
steps.stuck: If you get "Could not import workflow" on import, the JSON got cut off when copying. Copy with the copy button, not manual selection.

steps.title: Put your brand guide into both prompts
steps.where: n8n, Redactar pieza and Filtro de marca nodes
steps.action: In the Redactar pieza node, replace the blanks with your tone and your examples. In the Filtro de marca node, paste your rules from the guia_marca tab, one per line.
steps.expect: You run it with a test row and get back: a text that sounds like you and a brand verdict in JSON with apta true or false and reasons.
steps.stuck: If the filter approves everything, give it your guide's bad examples: "these sentences break the rules, if you see something similar the piece isn't approved." Contrast teaches it more than the rule alone.

steps.title: Test the approval circuit
steps.action: Run the workflow with two test pieces: a good one and one that breaks a rule on purpose (include a banned topic). The good one should arrive on Slack with buttons; the bad one should stay in brand_review with its reason in the sheet.
steps.expect: The Slack message carries the piece's full text, the date, and the network. You click approve and the row moves to approved; you click reject and it moves to discarded with a log.
steps.stuck: If the banned piece passes the filter, don't let it through "just this once": it's exactly the failure this step exists to catch. Strengthen the rule in the filter's prompt and retest.

steps.title: Break the workflow on purpose
steps.action: Run this kit's test cases: a row with no topic, an unparseable model response, two runs in a row on the same day. None of them should publish anything or corrupt the sheet.
steps.expect: The weird cases end up in coherent statuses with a reason. The double run doesn't duplicate pieces: the workflow only picks up planned status and changes it when it processes.
steps.stuck: If the double run duplicates, check that the first node after generating changes the row's status. That's your idempotency protection: a picked-up piece stops being available.

steps.title: Pilot week with manual scheduling
steps.action: Turn on the workflow Monday through Friday. Every approved piece you schedule yourself by hand in your scheduler, batching it on Friday. Note how much you correct and how long it takes.
steps.expect: A week published consistently and two numbers: minutes per piece (should be 3-5 for review) and correction rate.
steps.stuck: If you correct more than half the pieces, stop the workflow and go back to the prompt step: generating garbage faster isn't the goal. The pilot continues once the rate drops.

phases.title: Metrics, report, and handoff
phases.goal: Close the loop: measure what works, adjust the calendar with data, and leave the system explained so it survives without you.
phases.deliverable: Weekly metrics in the sheet, monthly report with decisions, and a handoff sheet tested by someone else.
done: Every piece's metrics are collected 7 days out, always the same way
There's a monthly report saying what to repeat and what to stop
Next month's calendar was built looking at the previous month's metrics
Someone else has operated the system for a week using the handoff sheet

steps.title: Set up metrics collection
steps.where: Your scheduler or each network's stats, and the sheet
steps.action: Every Monday, log into the metricas tab the data for pieces that turned 7 days old: reach, engagement, clicks. By hand at first: fifteen minutes. Add by hand any conversions you can attribute.
steps.expect: Every published piece ends up with its metrics row. In three weeks you can already compare pillars against each other.
steps.stuck: Don't compare a 2-day piece with a 30-day one: the fixed 7-day window exists for that. If you miss a Monday, note the real measurement date and keep going.

steps.title: Generate the monthly report
steps.action: At month's end, paste the pieces table with metrics and run the analysis prompt. Keep the three decisions, not the whole analysis.
steps.expect: Three concrete decisions: a type of piece to double down on, one to kill, a new experiment. With the numbers behind them.
steps.stuck: If the differences between pieces are small, don't force conclusions from a twenty-piece sample. Say "not enough signal yet" and wait another month: that's a valid conclusion.

steps.title: Recycle what worked
steps.where: Claude or ChatGPT, and your calendar
steps.action: Take the month's three highest-engagement pieces and run them through the recycling prompt: new versions, other formats, other angles on the same topic. Put the results into next month's calendar.
steps.expect: Every winning piece yields two or three new, already-planned pieces. Next month's calendar fills in half the time.
steps.stuck: Recycling isn't repeating: if the model gives back the same piece with synonyms, ask for "same topic, opposite angle" or "turn the tip into a common mistake."

steps.title: Write the handoff sheet and do the handover
steps.where: A document, and a real week
steps.action: Write how the system works: where the calendar is, how a piece is approved, how to stop the workflow, what to do if the model fails, and what to check every Monday. Then have someone else operate it for a full week without asking you.
steps.expect: A two-page sheet and a week of someone else operating it. What that person asks you is what's missing from the sheet.
steps.stuck: If you're a personal brand with no one else, do the handover with yourself: don't touch anything for a week except approving. If the system needs you daily for anything else, that's what's left to automate or document.

prompts.name: Generate the month's editorial calendar
prompts.when: Once a month, with last month's metrics in view if you have them.
prompts.prompt:
Act as [BUSINESS]'s content lead. We're going to build next month's editorial calendar, and I want specific rows for a spreadsheet, not loose ideas.

My strategy, which you can't change:
- Content pillars and their proportion: [PILLARS]
- Networks and frequency: [NETWORKS AND FREQUENCY]
- Tone: [TONE]
- Banned topics: [BANNED]

This month's context:
- Notable dates for my business this month (campaigns, events, season): [KEY DATES]
- What worked last month, if I know it: [WHAT WORKED]
- The questions my customers ask most: [FREQUENT QUESTIONS]

Calendar rules:
1. Give me back a table with exactly these columns: publish_date, network, pillar, topic, format. One row per piece, respecting my weekly frequency, not one piece more.
2. Every topic is a specific sentence that's almost a headline already. "3 mistakes I see every week when [TYPICAL ACTION]" works; "useful tips" doesn't.
3. Keep the pillar proportion within each week, not just across the month total.
4. My business's notable dates rule: place campaign pieces a few days before the date, not on the day itself.
5. No topic can touch the banned list, not even in passing.
6. Alternate formats: don't give me five carousels in a row.
7. Mark with the word EXPERIMENT a single piece for the month that tries something new (format or topic outside the pillars). One, not five.

After the table, tell me in three lines which pieces on the calendar seem weakest and why, so I can decide whether to change them. Don't explain the strategy to me: I already have it. Give me the table and that final note.

fill.what: What you are and what you sell, in one line
fill.example: a physiotherapy clinic in Zaragoza specializing in back pain

fill.what: Your pillars with proportion, from phase 1
fill.example: practical tips 50%, cases and results 30%, who we are 20%

fill.what: Where and how many times per week
fill.example: Instagram 3 pieces/week, Facebook 2 (reusing Instagram's)

fill.what: Your tone in one line with an example
fill.example: direct and friendly, informal: "pain isn't cured with a brace, it's cured by moving"

fill.what: Forbidden topics
fill.example: cure promises, politics, mentioning other clinics

fill.what: What's happening this month in your business
fill.example: on the 15th we open afternoon slots; week of the 20th, back-to-school

fill.what: Your two or three best recent pieces
fill.example: the desk-stretch reel (4,000 views) and the back-pain-myths carousel

fill.what: Your customers' real questions, they're gold for topics
fill.example: how many sessions do I need?, does a mat help at all?, is a back crack bad?

fill.what: Don't fill this in: it's part of the topic-format example
fill.example: leave it as-is in the prompt

prompts.expect: A table ready to paste into the sheet, with topics that are almost headlines already, pillar proportion respected, and a final note with the weak pieces.
prompts.stuck: If the topics come out generic, the problem is almost always an empty or thin [FREQUENT QUESTIONS]. Spend a week jotting down the literal questions people ask you and come back: the calendar changes category.

prompts.name: Draft a social media piece
prompts.when: This is the workflow's drafting node prompt. Also works by hand, piece by piece.
prompts.prompt:
You write [BUSINESS]'s social posts. Write a piece for the network and topic below. A person will review it before scheduling, but I want it to come out so finished that reviewing means reading and approving.

Tone guide. These three pieces of mine are your voice reference; imitate their rhythm, vocabulary, and attitude:
[EXAMPLES OF YOUR PIECES]

Certain data you can use. Anything not here does NOT exist, and prices, timelines, and promises are written exactly as given:
[FIXED DATA]

Hard rules:
- Forbidden to invent data, figures, testimonials, or results. If the topic calls for a fact you don't have, write MISSING DATA: and what's missing.
- Forbidden social-filler phrases: "don't miss out!", "what are you waiting for?", "tell us in the comments!" and family.
- Maximum [EMOJI] emoji. Zero is also valid.
- The first line has to stand on its own: it's the only thing visible before "see more." No "Today I bring you...".
- Banned topics, not even in passing: [BANNED]
- Close with a single, concrete call to action: [USUAL CTA]

Output format by network:
- If it's a post or reel: the caption text, and below it the line HASHTAGS: with [N HASHTAGS] specific hashtags (nothing like #love #instagood).
- If it's a carousel: CARD 1 through CARD [N CARDS], one strong sentence per card, and the caption separately.
- Always add at the end the IMAGE: line with a one-sentence description of the accompanying image or template.

The piece:
- Network: [NETWORK]
- Pillar: [PILLAR]
- Topic: [TOPIC]

Return only the piece with its format. No explanations, no alternative options, no questions to me.

fill.what: Who you are, in one line
fill.example: a physiotherapy clinic in Zaragoza

fill.what: Three real pieces of yours you like, pasted in full. The prompt's most important field
fill.example: "A brace won't fix your back. It'll get you used to not using the muscles that would..." (and two more)

legal: If you publish photos of customers, employees, or students, you need their explicit consent for that specific use. "They said it was fine" doesn't hold up: get it in writing, even a simple form.
Testimonials must be real and demonstrable. Making up reviews or testimonials with AI is deceptive advertising and, besides being sanctionable, is the kind of thing a competitor happily reports.

AI-generated content: check each platform's disclosure policies and your sector's rules. In regulated sectors (health, finance, legal, food), the claims in your posts are subject to sector-specific advertising rules: human review is also compliance review.

Image and music rights: don't use photos, videos, or music without a license. The platforms' own libraries (Instagram/TikTok music for business accounts) have limited commercial catalogs: check before building a reel around a song.
Contests and promotions have legal requirements (filed terms, clear conditions) and their own platform rules. Don't improvise a giveaway because the calendar had a gap.

If you keep data from people who write to you via messages or comments (names, phone numbers for a booking), that's data processing under GDPR: account for it in your records of processing activities and don't copy it into sheets everyone can see.
Label advertising as advertising. If a piece promotes a paid collaboration, mark it as such; advertising conduct rules apply just the same on a small feed.

Employees' personal brands: if you post on behalf of an organization, clarify who owns the accounts and the credentials. A company account on the personal phone of someone who leaves is a classic, avoidable problem.
This is practical guidance, not legal advice. If your sector is regulated or the campaign is large, have someone with a signature review it.

risks.risk: A piece with invented data gets published
risks.sign: A price, a timeline, or a result in a piece nobody remembers giving
risks.fix: The certain-data list in the drafting prompt, the brand filter checking numbers, and human approval. All three together: none alone is enough.

risks.sign: Pieces are correct but interchangeable with any competitor's; saves and comments drop
risks.fix: Refresh the prompt's tone examples every month with your best real pieces, and keep one fully hand-written piece a week. The system imitates your voice: if you stop having a voice, it imitates nothing.

risks.sign: Pieces expiring in pending_approval; the calendar publishes days late
risks.fix: A defined backup, an agreed deadline (48 hours), and the written rule: what's not reviewed in time falls off, it doesn't publish itself. Never turn silence into approval.

risks.sign: Zero corrections for weeks and approvals in seconds
risks.fix: The approval message shows the full text, not a link. And a monthly trap: deliberately include a piece with an error and check it gets caught. If it doesn't, the approval is theater.

risks.risk: The workflow dies silently and the account goes quiet
risks.sign: A week with no posts and nobody noticed until a client mentioned it
risks.fix: An alert if a business day generated no pieces while the calendar had planned rows, and another if the calendar has less than a week of rows ahead.

risks.risk: A scheduled piece goes stale before going out
risks.sign: A promo for a service you no longer offer gets published, or a cheerful piece on the day of a crisis
risks.fix: A quick review of the scheduled queue every Monday, and the handoff sheet saying how to unpublish in two minutes. Facing any external crisis, pause the whole queue first and ask questions later.

risks.risk: The account or API key gets exposed
risks.sign: Posts nobody made, or API usage at impossible hours
risks.fix: Keys only in n8n credentials, two-factor on every social account, and account credentials in a team password manager, not on someone's personal phone.

defend.question: What if AI publishes something stupid?
defend.answer: It can't: the system ends at an approval queue, not a publish button. Every piece goes through an automatic brand filter and then a person reads it and approves it, with their name and time logged. A piece that isn't approved doesn't exist for the public. The day something bad gets published, it'll be because a person approved it, and we'll know who and when: exactly like without AI, but logged.

defend.question: Doesn't it show that it's written by AI?
defend.answer: It shows when the prompt is empty. Ours carries real pieces from the brand as a voice example, a list of certain data, and forbidden phrases. And we measure it: the approver's correction rate is [X] out of ten pieces and dropping. When a piece sounds like a template, the filter flags it and it gets rewritten. Also, one piece a week is still one hundred percent human, on purpose.

defend.question: Why don't we publish automatically and skip the review?
defend.answer: Because the saving is three minutes per piece and the risk is a screenshot circulating forever. Human review costs half an hour a week; a piece with a made-up price or an illegal promise published on a Saturday costs far more. Automation is in generating and organizing, which is where the hours were going; approving was never the bottleneck.

defend.question: What do I get here that an agency doesn't give me?
defend.answer: The system is yours and stays in-house: the calendar, the brand guide, the prompts calibrated to your voice, and the metrics. If we stopped tomorrow, all of that stays yours and working. With an agency, when the agency leaves, the system leaves with it. Cost also doesn't scale with pieces: publishing double doesn't cost double.

defend.question: How do I know this works beyond likes?
defend.answer: The sheet has a conversions column: messages, bookings, or sales attributed to each piece. It's filled by hand and it's the monthly report's first figure. The 90-day success criterion we agreed on is [criterion], not followers. If at 90 days that figure hasn't moved, the report will say so plainly and we'll decide whether the problem is the content, the channel, or the offer.

defend.question: How much does it cost to maintain per month?
defend.answer: €[X] in tools and API — the model runs cents per piece, here's the math — plus about [Y] hours of a person's time: approving, scheduling on Friday, and the monthly review. That's half the hours that used to go into thinking up and writing every post from scratch, and it's measured with phase 1's stopwatch.

words: content pillar
A recurring master topic that repeats every week with different pieces. Three well-chosen pillars feed a year of calendar.
editorial calendar
The sheet with what's posted, when, where, and what status it's in. The kit's heart: the workflow only runs what the calendar says.
piece
Each individual post: a post, a carousel, a reel. One row in the calendar.
caption
The text accompanying a post. The first line decides whether anyone keeps reading.
brand filter
The automatic review that checks a piece against your rules before a person sees it. Saves reviewing the obviously bad; replaces nobody.
tone guide
Real examples of your voice pasted into the prompt. Works better than any list of adjectives.
reach
How many distinct accounts saw the piece. Useful to compare pieces against each other, not to pay the bills.
conversion
The action that does pay the bills: a message, a booking, a sale attributed to a piece. Noted by hand and the metric that rules.
schedule
Leaving an approved piece with a date and time for the platform to publish on its own. Scheduling is automatic; approving, never.
recycle
Getting new pieces out of one that worked: another angle, another format, another network. Not repeating it with synonyms.
